title: Hybrids vary little in the first generation but greatly in later generations

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Hybrids vary little in the first generation but greatly in later generations

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Hybrids are only slightly variable in the first generation but extremely variable in succeeding generations, because the reproductive system of the hybrids themselves is disturbed.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The slight degree of variability in hybrids from the first cross or in the first generation, in contrast with their extreme variability in the succeeding generations, is a curious fact and deserves attention.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter VIII, “Hybridism”; section “Hybrids and mongrels compared independently of their fertility”. Scope: plant and animal hybrids bred over several generations

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch08-13: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.78

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Generation-specific segregation variance is a standard quantitative-genetic measurement with many public mapping populations. The pattern is resolvable now, while Darwin's causal wording is only partly addressed.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure phenotypic variance in F1, F2, and later hybrid generations under common conditions, then compare generation-specific variance. Low F1 and substantially higher segregating-generation variance support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The proposed cause is less directly tested than the variance pattern.

Environmental variance and parental divergence affect contrasts.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.79
operationalizability: 0.94
data adequacy: 0.58
analysis feasibility: 0.76
discriminating power: 0.8

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public mapping populations record both phenotypes across hybrid generations and markers that identify the cause of the extra variance. The pattern Darwin reported is therefore decidable, and the disturbed-reproduction explanation can be separated from ordinary segregation. Coverage is a subset of all hybrids but includes both plants and animals at a scale a small team can analyze with standard quantitative genetics.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare phenotypic variance of F1 hybrids with variance in F2 and later generations, and inspect marker segregation. Much greater later-generation variance confirms the pattern; equal variance refutes it. Segregation of intact parental alleles refutes a disturbed reproductive system as the cause, whereas chaotic gamete failure would support that cause.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Mapping populations are richer for crops and model animals than for arbitrary hybrids.

Later-generation variance also rises because of recombination even when fertility is normal, which is the alternative cause.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: If first-generation hybrids are only slightly variable while later generations are extremely variable, then in an experimental cross the phenotypic variance of F2 hybrids should exceed that of F1 hybrids for most measured traits, and F1 variance should be no greater than that of the parental species.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The artificial-cross table was read; 21 continuous traits had >= 8 F1 and F2 plants. For each trait the mean-scaled variance (variance of log values, or variance over squared mean for traits with zeros) was computed in F1 (n = 81 plants) and F2 (n = 36 plants); the median F2/F1 ratio and an exact sign test on the number of traits with ratio > 1 were evaluated against the pre-registered thresholds. F1 variance was also compared with both parental species.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Dataset: Dryad doi:10.25338/B8QS5T (Cakile edentula x C. maritima artificial crosses with F1, F2 and backcross generations; CC0). For every continuous trait recorded for both F1 and F2 individuals from the artificial crosses (identified from the data files after download; traits with < 8 individuals in either generation are excluded), compute the variance of log-transformed values (equivalent to a squared coefficient of variation for positive traits; for traits with zero or negative values use the variance of the trait divided by its squared mean) in F1 and in F2. Primary statistic: the median across traits of the variance ratio F2/F1. Pass ('supports') if the median ratio is >= 1.5 AND the F2 variance exceeds the F1 variance in a majority of traits with an exact binomial sign-test p < 0.05. 'Mixed' if F2 exceeds F1 in a majority of traits with p < 0.05 but the median ratio is between 1.0 and 1.5 (more variable, but not 'extremely' so relative to F1), or if the median ratio is >= 1.5 but the sign test is not significant. The comparison of F1 variance with parental variance is reported as an extra and does not enter the verdict.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Refuted if F2 hybrids are not more variable than F1 hybrids: the median F2/F1 variance ratio is <= 1.0, or F2 exceeds F1 in half or fewer of the traits. If the archive cannot be downloaded, the verdict is 'inconclusive' with reason 'data-unavailable'.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: median across traits of the F2/F1 ratio of mean-scaled phenotypic variance

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: 11 of 21 traits with ratio > 1; exact sign-test p = 0.5000; ratio range 0.03-8.01

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Darwin's 'variable' is read as phenotypic variance among individuals of the same hybrid generation raised under common conditions, scaled by the trait mean so that traits of different magnitude are comparable. 'First generation' = F1 (cross between the two species), 'succeeding generations' = F2 (F1 x F1); backcrosses are not used because Darwin's statement concerns hybrids bred inter se. The claim's causal clause (disturbed reproductive system of the hybrids) is not tested; the quantitative-genetic explanation (segregation of parental alleles in F2) would produce the same pattern and is the modern reinterpretation. One plant cross is tested; the claim is stated for plant and animal hybrids generally.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: Asymmetry in fitness-related traits of later-generation hybrids between two invasive species (Cakile edentula x C. maritima), file Chengjun_Experiment.csv

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The outcome (median F2/F1 variance ratio between 1.0 and 1.5 with a bare, non-significant majority of traits more variable in F2) fell in a gap of the pre-registered decision rule; it is recorded as 'mixed'. By trait the pattern is strongly heterogeneous: floral and plant-size traits are 3-8 times more variable in F2, whereas seed mass, germination, phenology and fruit/seed counts are less variable in F2 than in F1.

A single interspecific plant cross with 36 F2 plants; Darwin's generalisation covers many plant and animal hybrids.

F1 plants come from many independent parental pairs (families), which adds between-family variance to F1 that a single-pair F1 would not have; this biases against the claim.

Mean-scaled variance compares dispersion across traits of different units but is sensitive to small means for count traits.

Environmental variance in a common garden is included in both generations and cannot be separated from segregational variance here.

The claim's causal clause (disturbed reproductive system of hybrids) is not tested; Mendelian segregation in F2 is the modern explanation of the same pattern.
